title: Warmup eigenspectrum profiling - microburst attenuation probe (scratch)
content:
Context and quick motivation:
- Trying to understand why short microbursts (<2s) after an idle period spike p99 despite overall warm-cache behavior being fine. Suspect that the distribution of early KV-cache activations + small kernel dispatch patterns cause transient tail events.
- Idea: treat the activation vectors seen during warmup as a dynamic signal, compute an approximated eigenspectrum to quantify how "concentrated" the early-token activation subspace is vs steady-state. Hypothesis: sharper low-rank energy early leads to less efficient batching/kernels -> higher variance in per-token execution time.

Experiment ID: WEP-2024-02-18-A
Run owner: Karthik
Hardware: 1x A100-sxm4 (40GB) in single-tenant test node
Model: rwi-7b-v2 (fp16 runtime path, qkv-cache enabled)
Serving runtime commit: git@github.com:redwood/serving-runtime@a7c9f2b
Workload harness: local loadgen (poisson arrival, adjustable burst factor)
Input profile: 16–64 token prompt lengths, average request tokens = 28
Batching config: max_batch = 16, dynamic_batch_timeout_ms = 8, prefill_cache = true
KV-cache priming: enabled (cold to warm transition logged)
Trace instrumentation: per-kernel timing + per-request enqueue/dequeue timestamps + activation snapshot dump for first 8 tokens (L2 downsampled)

Method:
1) Play repeated microbursts: 5s idle -> 1s burst @ 120% of steady qps -> 10s ramp down, repeat 60 cycles.
2) For each request in first 3 tokens after idle, capture activation snapshot (float32, downsampled to 512 dims) from layer 10.
3) Compute SVD on minibatch of 128 snapshots every cycle; take top-10 singular values, normalize by sum -> call this "warm-spectrum".
4) Correlate per-cycle warm-spectrum concentration (s1 / sum(s)) with p50/p95/p99 latencies for the same cycle.

Raw observations (selected cycles):
- cycle 4: s1_norm=0.43, p50=32ms, p95=86ms, p99=210ms
- cycle 11: s1_norm=0.12, p50=28ms, p95=64ms, p99=92ms
- cycle 19: s1_norm=0.51, p50=36ms, p95=120ms, p99=320ms (notable outlier)
- cycle 27: s1_norm=0.09, p50=26ms, p95=58ms, p99=88ms
- cycle 43: s1_norm=0.38, p50=30ms, p95=78ms, p99=190ms

Aggregated stats over 60 cycles (first-token requests only):
- mean(s1_norm) = 0.29
- stdev(s1_norm) = 0.14
- Pearson r(s1_norm, p99) = 0.61
- Pearson r(s1_norm, p95) = 0.48
- Pearson r(s1_norm, p50) = 0.21

Interpretation:
- Moderate to strong correlation between concentration of early activations (higher s1_norm) and tail latency (p99). Intuition: when activations concentrate into a smaller subspace, kernel codepaths produce less uniform work distribution across threads/warps, causing some threads to take longer. Also observed increased small dispatches (more kernel launches of short duration) during those cycles.
- Not every high s1_norm cycle produced high p99; correlated with small batch sizes (avg batch size <=3) during that cycle. So a two-factor effect: concentrated eigenspectrum + tiny batch sizes amplify tails.

Short ascii histogram of s1_norm distribution (60 cycles):
0.0-0.1: |||||| (6)
0.1-0.2: |||||||||| (11)
0.2-0.3: |||||||| (8)
0.3-0.4: |||||| (6)
0.4-0.5: |||| (4)
0.5-0.6: | (1)

Micro-trace example (cycle 19):
- enqueue->dispatch skew: mean enqueue->launch = 3.7ms (vs baseline 1.1ms)
- per-kernel run times: kernelA: 9.2ms (2x baseline), kernelB: 1.1ms, kernelC: 0.6ms
- observed 12 kernel launches for 8 requests (vs 5 typical) -> overhead increases

Quick root-cause hypothesis:
1) Model warmup states with high low-rank energy cause attention/qkv matmuls to have short, cache-misaligned slices resulting in kernel fragmentation.
2) When batch size is small, the relative cost of a fragmented kernel launch is large -> p99 increases.
3) Prefill cache helps average case but doesn't remove the initial spectral concentration effect.

Mitigation experiments to run next (short list):
- M1: Increase dynamic_batch_timeout_ms from 8 -> 20 to allow slightly larger batches during microbursts. Measure impact on p99 and on average latency.
- M2: Force mini-batching grouping at pre-dispatch layer (aggregate up to 8 short requests arriving within 6ms) to reduce kernel launches.
- M3: On-device micro-kernel fusion patch (experimental in branch: GH:repo/PR#892) to reduce fragmentation cost.
- M4: Embedding a small random jitter to ingress arrival (±3ms) to avoid pathological synchronized arrivals.

Quick tradeoffs/concerns:
- Increasing batch timeout reduces p99 but will add p50 cost for interactive workloads; need SLI tradeoff.
- Kernel fusion patch shows promise in microbenchmarks but requires careful GPU occupancy testing for different sequence lengths.

Notes to self / action items:
- Run M1 + M4 in combination for 30-cycle run and record eigenspectrum again (target date: 2024-03-04).
- Share this note with Riley and Mira and schedule 30-min sync to pick which mitigation to graduate to a canary.
- Add lightweight per-cycle logging into canary harness: s1_norm, avg_batch_size, kernel_launch_count, p99 (first-token). Keep retention 14 days for analysis.
- Follow up linking: add GH:repo/PR#892 benchmarking artifacts to the PR and reference JIRA INF-2193.

Rough TL;DR (for slack):
- Found correlation between concentrated early activation eigenspectrum and p99 spikes during short microbursts. Amplified when batch sizes are tiny.
- Short-term mitigations: slightly longer dynamic batching timeout + small ingress jitter. Medium-term: micro-kernel fusion.

Raw experiment notes appended to s3 (internal): s3://redwood-test-logs/bench/wep/2024-02-18-A/ (snapshots + svd dumps + telemetry CSVs)

End of scratchpad.
